messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: multivariate normal density
parts:
Hi,

In src/stan/prob/distributions/multi_normal.hpp , there are two
parameterizations of the multivariate normal distribution. The first
takes mu and Sigma, while the second takes mu and L, where L is a
Cholesky factor of Sigma. I believe it would be much better --- faster
and more numerically accurate --- if the first simply calculated L and
called the second.

There are three slow and inaccurate things in the first, more
textbookish, implementation. First, the check_cov_matrix() function
checks Sigma for squareness, symmetry, and sufficient positivity of
its eigenvalues. Second, the determinant of Sigma is calculated.
Third, the inverse of Sigma is calculated. Neither the determinant nor
the inverse calculation exploit the positive definiteness of Sigma.
Also, if one were going to calculate the eigendecomposition of a
matrix, you would already have the ingredients for the determinant and
the inverse. But the eigendecomposition is worse than the Cholesky
decomposition anyway.

The Cholesky decomposition in Eigen does some checking and has
a .info() method to check whether something went wrong numerically.
So, you could just do Sigma.llt(), verify the .info(), and pass
the .matrixL() to the second implementation of the density.

But, is there any currently any route to the multivariate normal
density that doesn't construct Sigma from the
stan::prob::read_cov_matrix() function? If there is no such route,
then it isn't necessary to check whether Sigma is square, symmetric,
or positive definite. And, I can easily change things so that there is
a way to return L instead of Sigma := L * L.transpose() because L is a
function of the primative parameters that gets calculated anyways. In
which case, we could just call the second multivariate normal density
implementation directly.

I realize we are not overly concerned about performance for a 1.0
release, but the multivariate normal is so common and this looks like
a very low hanging fruit. Is there a more subtle reason for the way
the code is now?

Ben

Yes. Stan's syntax checker only makes sure
the argument's a matrix.

What I'd really like to be able to do for some
of these complex distributions is to only call
a solver once if the matrix is a constant.

Right now, there's not a good way to parameterize
that in Stan.

What I want is the equivalent of an eager evaluation
at model construct time for constants and a lazy
evaluation for the other arguments.

So with a Normal(y|mu,Sigma), for instance, if
Sigma were a Matrix<double> rather than Matrix<var>,
I'd like to get all the solving monkey business out of
the way up front and then call something like
Normal_Sigma(y|mu).

Taking this idea even further, we'd pull loop-constant
calcs out of loops. Right now, we're thinking of
vectorizing some common cases by hard coding them,
but it'd be nice to have a way to do it in the language
when performance matters.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: multivariate normal density
parts: Hi Daniel,

On Jan 9, 9:59 pm, Daniel Lee <bear...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> Good points. The answer is that we haven't had the time to go through
> and optimize. If you want to go through and change the implementation,
> please feel free to. We have unit tests at:
> src/test/prob/distributions/multi_normal_test.cpp and
> src/test/agrad/distributions/multi_normal_test.cpp
OK, I will soon.

> Regarding the checks, that's something I think we should leave in.
> Perhaps we can work in a lighter check, but I won't make the
> assumption that stan::prob::read_cov_matrix() is the only way this
> function is called.

Perhaps another way to ask the question is whether a parameterized
covariance matrix should ever be allowed to get to the multivariate
normal density evaluation without coming from some sort of a
decomposition that ensures positive definiteness by construction. The
case where Sigma is a constant that Bob alluded to is a different
animal. The only scenario I can think of is if stan ever does
rejection sampling.

But the .llt() method will check that Sigma is square. And I think it
is the case that if Sigma is not symmetric and positive definite up to
some numerical tolerance, then .info() is supposed to indicate a
problem, but this may not be 100% guaranteed. The .ldlt() method is a
bit more reliable, but you have to be careful when using it for
statistical purposes because Eigen uses pivoting. So, I think it would
be okay for the first implementation of the density to do one of these
two Cholesky decompositions, check the .info(), and call the second
implementation.

If there were some reason to do the eigendecomposition, then just do
it inside the density function, use the eigenvalues to calculate the
determinant, and use the reciprocal eigenvalues to calculate the
inverse (rather than calling check_cov_matrix(Sigma),
determinant(Sigma) and inverse(Sigma) separately).

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: multivariate normal density
parts:
Another way to restate the issue is: What, if anything, prevents the
user from

0) Declaring a vector in the parameters block called covariances
1) Declaring a matrix in the derived parameters block called Sigma
2) Stuffing these covariances into Sigma with a nested for loop
3) Using that Sigma in a multivariate normal density in the model
block (along with some priors over the covariances)
4) Presuming that stan will magically do something reasonable if a
realization of Sigma were not an admissible covariance matrix.

If the answer is that multi_normal_log() throws a runtime error if
Sigma is inadmissible, then I could see why we need to check Sigma
thoroughly on every iteration. But I think it would be better if this
could be a compile-time error so that multi_normal_log() can be as
fast as possible.

WTFDBUGSD?

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: multivariate normal density
parts:
On 1/9/12 11:02 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Another way to restate the issue is: What, if anything, prevents the
> user from
>
> 0) Declaring a vector in the parameters block called covariances
> 1) Declaring a matrix in the derived parameters block called Sigma
> 2) Stuffing these covariances into Sigma with a nested for loop
> 3) Using that Sigma in a multivariate normal density in the model
> block (along with some priors over the covariances)

Nothing at all. The following's legal:

----------------------
parameters {
cov_matrix(5) Sigma;
...
}
derived parameters {
matrix(5,5) Omega;
for (m in 1:M)
for (n in 1:N)
Omega[m,n] = Sigma[m,n];
...
}
model {
y ~ multi_normal(mu,Omega);
}
------------------

(I'm about to rename "derived parameters" to
"transformed parameters".)

You can also replace that nested for loop
with a simple "Omega = Sigma;".

> 4) Presuming that stan will magically do something reasonable if a
> realization of Sigma were not an admissible covariance matrix.

Suppose you assigned to Omega in such a way that
it is not positive definite. In the code
as written above, the call to multi_normal_log(),
which happens per leapfrog step, will throw
an exception.

If instead you declared Omega as cov_matrix(5), then
there will be a check right after the derived parameters
are calculated which will throw an exception.

>
> If the answer is that multi_normal_log() throws a runtime error if
> Sigma is inadmissible,

Daniel's incorporated Boost error policies, so we can
configure multi_normal_log() to do whatever we want.
We want it to throw an exception.

A sampler can then decide to just treat an exception
like a rejection, or it can abort.

> then I could see why we need to check Sigma
> thoroughly on every iteration. But I think it would be better if this
> could be a compile-time error so that multi_normal_log() can be as
> fast as possible.

Given the flexibility noted above, we can't check
semantic constraints at compile time.

I suppose we could do something like you're suggesting
if we restrict the operations applied to covariance
matrices to be positive-definiteness preserving.
We can do assignment, we can rescale variances per
dimension -- what else?

It'd be some effort to code as I'd have to push more
information than dimensionality through to the semantic
type checker on the Stan side.

My plan right now (in fact, that's what I sat down
at the computer to do) is:

program, statement, and expression well-typedness:
Stan compile time (catch errors before C++)

data:
constraints checked on data as it's read in

transformed data:
constraints checked after transformed data
blocks calculates transformed data

parameters:
initial values checked as read in
?? per leapfrog step (after model statement)
final values checked per sample during write

transformed parameters:
?? per leapfrog step
final values checked per sample during write

local variables:
can't be declared as constrained, no checks

derived quantities:
checked per sample after calculated

expressions/functions:
dimensional well-formedness at compile time
constraints on values checked as functions are applied
(data read time for transformed data,
per leapfrog step for transformed params and model,
per sample for derived quantities)

The checks marked with ?? are the ones that would
really slow things down.


> WTFDBUGSD?

WTF does BUGS do? It's closed source, so we'd have
to ask. I think JAGS is using the R density
libs, so probably whatever R does. I don't know how
configurable that is.

One of the reasons we wrote Stan was because BUGS and JAGS
are not very good with covariance matrix parameters.

We had to write our own density libs so that we could
separately template out each arg for auto-dif.

>
> Ben

- Bob

P.S. I sort of like top-posting. Everyone gripes about it, but
with enough context, I prefer it. What do you all think?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: multivariate normal density
parts:
Ben's right -- there's no way to tell the
difference between plain old user error in
an ad-hoc covariance matrix construction,
arithmetic issues in the same, and arithmetic
issues in a sequence of ops that's supposed
to maintain positive definiteness (given arbitrary
precision).

If we have operations that are supposed to
maintain positive definiteness, I'd make it those
operations' responsibilities to maintain positive
definiteness.

Matt already added a bit of this fudging to some
of the log/logit calcs. We don't want our users
to be reduced to the inelegant BUGS/JAGS solution
of:

x <- max(0,min(1,inv_logit(...)))

It would be useful, at least for the multivariate normal,
to have a simple function:

double transpose_multiply2(vector x, matrix y) {
return x.transpose() * y * x;
}

(I can't think of a good name for this operation -- help?)

For one, it'd minimize promotion of doubles to
auto-dif variables in matrix ops, which would otherwise,
if x is data, involve the promotion of the
row vector x.transpose() and original vector x.

We'd probably need a second version if we went with
the maintain-positive-definiteness guarantee.

When JAGS hits a NaN, it sometimes logs and sometimes
crashes. I'm not sure what the conditions are. I'd
guess a limited number of retries then failure.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: multivariate normal density
parts:
I'd agree that operators should be responsible for maintaining
positive definiteness, but should they trust that the matrix they are
given is positive definite or should they check it? For a function
like

> double transpose_multiply2(vector x, matrix y) {
> return x.transpose() * y * x;
> }

if y is PD, then the result is guaranteed to be positive, but how does
it know that y is PD if a user might do something that calls it on a
matrix they made up? This is why I was wondering if we need some
internal classes like symmetricMatrix or psdMatrix that can be trusted
to be symmetric or PSD because they are instantiated by a responsible
constructor within stan. Then, we can have safer functions that are
defined for a plain Matrix that check once per iteration whether a
matrix that should be symmetric or PSD or whatever, is so.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: multivariate normal density
parts: I conflated multiple issues. Yes,

> double transpose_multiply2(vector x, matrix y) {
> return x.transpose() * y * x;
> }

should exist because it would be used by any elliptical distribution.
Although the above would actually be a subtle compiler error because
x.transpose() * y * x is a 1x1 matrix, whereas the calling function
wants the scalar ( x.transpose() * y * x)[0]. But if it were

> Matrix<T, dynamic, dynamic> transpose_multiply2(MatrixXd x, Matrix<T, dynamic, dynamic> y) {
> check_psd(y);

> return x.transpose() * y * x;
> }

the resulting matrix would be PSD (up to numerical tolerance) if y is
but neither have any PSD branding. If it were

> psdMatrix<T, dynamic, dynamic> transpose_multiply2(MatrixXd x, psdMatrix<T, dynamic, dynamic> y) {
> return y.multiplyonbothsides(x);
> }

then we don't need to check whether y is PSD but do need the
symmetricMatrix and psdMatrix classes, plus constructors,
documentation, etc.

Ben
